Chippa Football Academy

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take a deep dive into the newly named Africa School of Excellence, and find out why former staff and parents are blowing the whistle on Chippa Mpengesi.

Unique Selling Point:
The Transnet Football School of Excellence in Kempton Park has been handed over to controversial businessman and Chippa FC owner, Chippa Mpengesi. In just two months, the once proud legacy of this birthplace of champions has been decimated.
Staff and coaches have been fired, salaries have not paid, and the boys were left sleeping on the floor, eating 2-minute noodles.


Summary:
Transnet School of Excellence was founded in 1994 as a joint venture between Transnet and SAFA, run by a Board of Trustees. The Trustees included Transnet, SAFA, SAFCOC, Department of Basic Education, a representative of the Community and a representative of the Private Sector.

In 2020 the Trust was dissolved and the school was taken over by the Transnet Foundation as part of its CSI responsibilities. Transnet donated R20 m annually to run the school. Last year they decided they could not continue and put out a call for new sponsors. Some sponsors stepped forward and requested Financial Records for the school. NO FINANCIALS AVAILABLE. In August 2025 they published a tender as Request for Proposals, asking for a donor to take over the SOE.

They had five bids, including Pitso Mosimane who runs a very successful academy partnering with Curro schools; Thulani Majola a controversial businessman who was previously in liquidation, and Chippa Training Academy (Pty) Ltd, a company belonging to Chippa Mpengesi. One of the criteria was a proven track record educating high school pupils. But, the Chippa Training Academy is a company that trains security guards. What due diligence did Transnet do?
The only evidence of a school is social media calls for enrolment at the Chippa Academy in East London in July 2025. The school never opened. Instead, those pupils from the Eastern Cape have been bused to the Germiston campus.


Further information:
The school was handed over on 8 December 2025 amidst much fanfare. It only opened on 26 January as they were renovating the hostels. The teachers were paid late with no payslips, and no deductions. They went to the CCMA and were subsequently fired.
The matric students only started classed in the 2nd week of February. Last week every teacher and coach was asked to take a 95% salary reduction or face retrenchment. Everyone, including the Principal, was “retrenched”.

There is a new school Manager called Dr Maharaswa, a former Deputy DG at the Department of Basic Education. She has been banned from tendering for government contracts until 2030 because of fraud and corruption at the MICTSETA. She is now in charge of the school, accompanied by an armed bodyguard.

Many parents have removed their children, and those that remain are now expected to buy uniforms manufactured by Chippa’s company RADA at a cost of R5000. They are also expected to pay school fees of R9200 per month. Previously this was a school for underprivileged, hugely talented kids, and everything was free.

Apart from the "elite football academy", the school claims to offer "Academic Excellence. Core subjects and enrichment programs that challenge learners and prepare them for top-tier universities." But just last week Chippa was heard telling the boys they should become security guards.


Extra Budget Items:
Possible travel to East London for interviews with Chippa Mpengesi and former parents.

FOOTBALL SCHOOL FALLOUT


(Govan) The SAFA/Transnet Football School of Excellence – the cradle of champions - founded on the East Rand in 1994 to nurture underprivileged talent. Every year thousands of children from dusty township soccer pitches around the country would compete for just 20 places. Those selected enjoyed full scholarships from Grade 8 to matric, and top-notch coaching that produced the best of the best.

(Parent) Guys like Steven Pienaar, and you know Bryce Moon, Bernard Parker, they’re all from there.

(Govan) Hundreds of boys have passed through these hallowed halls, sponsored by Transnet to the tune of R20 million a year. But now there’s a new owner, and most staff and coaches have been replaced.

(Gilbert Molala) Within a period of three months, you’ve done away with more than 20 people. That’s ridiculous!

(Govan) Nervous parents are left wondering if their children will pass the year.

(Parent) We received videos of our children sleeping in class. They were tired and there’s no-one to teach them.

(Parent) It used to be a proper school. I don’t know anymore. I can’t tell.

(Govan) This is the field of dreams, a place where raw talent could be your ticket to the big leagues. But now, the pride of South African soccer faces huge challenges – and its legacy is in danger of collapse.

(Govan) Transnet can no longer finance this community development project, so last year they requested proposals for a new donor to own and operate the school. This donor would have to pay R21 million a year to cover costs.
First on the bidders list was Chippa Training Academy, an Eastern Cape company that offers skills training, mainly for security guards. It’s often been in the news for all the wrong reasons. The director is Siviwe ‘Chippa’ Mpengesi, owner of Chippa United Football Club. This larger-than-life character heads up a multimillion-rand business empire, but there are persistent reports of tender irregularities and unpaid salaries. His staff call him Chairman.
(Subtitles) This is Chairman Chippa Mpengesi’s story of belief. When others saw a school about to close, he saw a field of dreams.

(Govan) Strangely, the school wasn’t awarded to Chippa Training Academy, but another entity in his stable called Chipcor Developers. Transnet CEO handed over the school to him in December.

(Gertina van der Merwe) He made a speech.

(Govan) What did he say?

(Gertina van der Merwe) Oh, the school won’t change. And the CEO also said the school won’t change, and it will continue the way it is, and so on.

(Govan) Gertina van der Merwe taught at the school for 17 years. As Head of Department, she was concerned when the school opened two weeks late in January.

(Gertina van der Merwe) I was astonished because for matric that is quite a serious problem.

(Govan) Why was the school only opening on the 26th?

(Gertina van der Merwe) They were refurbishing the residence.

(Govan) The buildings were given a facelift, and the bathrooms upgraded. But changes at the newly named Africa School of Excellence are more than cosmetic.

(Gilbert Molala) Ten teachers, all of them are gone. It’s only…including myself.

(Govan) Gilbert Molala was the principal of the school for five years but hasn’t been back since the 11th of March.

(Gilbert Molala) The chairman told me that I’m earning too much money, then he cannot afford me.

(Dr Maharswa) You have a principal that earns R74000 per month, but who does not teach a single class.

(Govan) The Head of Transition in charge of restructuring the school is Dr Maboreng Maharaswa. She claims the staff were overpaid.

(Govan) So, the options for the staff were take the salary cut or get retrenched?

(Dr Maharaswa) Yes.

(Govan) And you think that’s fair?

(Dr Maharaswa) It was fair because it wasn’t compulsory retrenchment. They had the choice to either stay or go.

(Govan) These boys are bidding farewell to two teachers who were offered a 95% salary cut when their positions were deemed redundant. But Maharaswa was already recruiting their replacements.
We met one of the teachers who asked us to hide his face.

(Govan) So, they were asking you to downgrade your pay to R2000?

(Teacher) Yes.

(Govan) Were you being overpaid?

(Teacher) No, it’s a benchmark of a government pay.

(Govan) So, what could be the reason for wanting to drop your salary if it’s not inflated?

(Teacher) The fact that maybe the company does not have money.

(Govan) The retrenchees were told the business faces a crisis, and they still haven’t been paid out.

(Govan) How can you face a crisis if you knew how much it would cost and Transnet believed you have the money to run this school?

(Dr Maharaswa) Yes, and it is still the case, but our projections are that if we continued with that dispensation, running the school is going to require much more than twenty million.

(Chippa subtitles) Everything here is on my shoulders. Okay, teachers? I don’t get any subsidy, no allowance from government; nothing!

(Govan) Tough financial decisions make sense in a corporate environment, but in a school, cost-cutting impacts the children. And given what we’re about to tell you, it’s clear who’s paying the price.

(Parent) The food is too little. You can't even see the chicken, which part of the chicken they are eating.

(Govan) Chipcor got the school on condition all boys already enrolled would continue to be fully sponsored. That’s why their parents are afraid to complain openly.

(Parent) My son sent me a picture of two Weetbix without milk. Most of the time they have two-minute noodles with a little bit of veggies in there.

(Dr Maharaswa) They stay for free. They eat for free, four meals per day.

(Govan) Are they eating two-minute noodles?

(Dr Maharaswa) No, actually the noodles is what we see elsewhere.

(Govan) On a guided tour of the pantry, we couldn’t help noticing an empty box of instant noodles. Parents of newly enrolled boys are now paying R97 000 a year. But who’s teaching them?

(Dr Maharaswa) Qualified educators with relevant specialisations.

(Govan) Are these teachers who are fresh out of university or do they have experience teaching?

(Dr Maharaswa) The majority of them are fresh out of university.

(Govan) How much are you paying the new teachers?

(Dr Maharaswa) R16 000 per month.

(Govan) Is that an entry-level salary for a teacher?

(Dr Maharaswa) It is, it is.

(Gertina van der Merwe) You can't pay a teacher peanuts and expect high performance.

(Govan) After a heated argument with Dr Maharaswa, Mrs van der Merwe was given a disciplinary hearing and summarily dismissed.

(Gertina van der Merwe) My honest opinion is that the kids are going to fail.

(Parent) You want now cheap labour, cheap labour that will come with a risk of our children’s education.

(Govan) The matrics only received their Term One reports this week, and the Gauteng Department of Education is investigating if the curriculum has been covered. But there’s a more serious matter.

(Govan) All independent schools in South Africa have to be registered and accredited with Umalusi, the Council for Quality Assurance. When a school has a change ownership, principal, or its name, Umalusi has to be notified within 14 days. That never happened in this case, which means the Africa School of Excellence is not accredited.

(Govan) The school is still relying on the original registration and there’s a photocopy of the certificate hanging in the entrance hall.

(Govan) Why didn't you notify Umalusi about the change of ownership and the change of name of the school?

(Dr Maharaswa) But there has not been a change of ownership of this entity.

(Govan) There has been a change of ownership.

(Dr Maharaswa) No.

(Govan) Chipcor Developers owns the school.

(Dr Maharaswa) No, they operate the school.

(Govan) Who owns the school?

(Dr Maharaswa) Pardon?

(Govan) Who owns the school?

(Dr Maharaswa) It's the same entity that it used to own, but we’re operating the school.

(Govan) And the school's name has not changed?

(Dr Maharaswa) Pardon? The school's name has not...the school's registered name has not changed. We are changing the trading name.

(Govan) If you've been charging school fees for this school that's not accredited with Umalusi, that would be fraud.

(Dr Maharaswa) That would be, but luckily our school is accredited with Umalusi.

(Govan) But accreditation is not transferable between different owners, and Umalusi told Carte Blanche that Africa School of Excellence is not currently accredited.

(Govan) But Dr Maharaswa herself is associated with fraud and corruption, after an R11.2 million contract was improperly awarded to her company Northern Lights 371. Her business partner’s uncle was CEO of the SETA at the time and was fired after an investigation.

(Govan) Have you ever been accused of fraud personally?

(Dr Maharaswa) I don’t think that’s relevant to the interview. The interview is about the school.

(Govan) We believe that you’ve been banned from doing tenders with the State for ten years. Is that right?

(Dr Maharaswa) That is a matter that is being challenged. It’s under review.

(Govan) When Transnet put out requests for proposals, one of its conditions was successful bidder’s tax matters be in order. It’s been widely reported that Chippa Mpengesi owes SARS R53 million in unpaid taxes. We wanted to ask Transnet how they did their due diligence, but they declined an interview.

(Govan) Chippa has called those reports misleading, but Transnet confirmed that during the tender process they flagged a matter related to his tax compliance.

(Govan) Transnet say they had a robust, open and competitive procurement process, but they deny that Chippa Training Academy submitted a bid for the school. This contradicts their own tender records submitted to Treasury.

(Govan) Transnet say they are transferring the relevant assets to Chipcor, but do they mean the vehicles and school equipment, or the buildings and the 12-hectare property?

(Govan) Carte Blanche has now requested the full record of decision on this tender, to understand why a hundred schoolboys were entrusted to the care of this flamboyant, but compromised personality.

(Govan) Chippa never responded to our interview request.

And the CEO also said the school won’t change, and it will continue the way it is, and so on. (Govan) Gertina van der Merwe taught at the school for 17 years. As Head of Department, she was concerned when the school opened two weeks late in January. (Gertina van der Merwe) I was astonished because for matric that is quite a serious problem. (Govan) Why was the school only opening on the 26th? (Gertina van der Merwe) They were refurbishing the residence. (Govan) The buildings were given a facelift, and the bathrooms upgraded. But changes at the newly named Africa School of Excellence are more than cosmetic. (Gilbert Molala) Ten teachers, all of them are gone. It’s only…including myself. (Govan) Gilbert Molala was the principal of the school for five years but hasn’t been back since the 11th of March. (Gilbert Molala) The chairman told me that I’m earning too much money, then he cannot afford me. (Dr Maharswa) You have a principal that earns R74000 per month, but who does not teach a single class. (Govan) The Head of Transition in charge of restructuring the school is Dr Maboreng Maharaswa. She claims the staff were overpaid. (Govan) So, the options for the staff were take the salary cut or get retrenched? (Dr Maharaswa) Yes. (Govan) And you think that’s fair? (Dr Maharaswa) It was fair because it wasn’t compulsory retrenchment. They had the choice to either stay or go. (Govan) These boys are bidding farewell to two teachers who were offered a 95% salary cut when their positions were deemed redundant. But Maharaswa was already recruiting their replacements. We met one of the teachers who asked us to hide his face. (Govan) So, they were asking you to downgrade your pay to R2000? (Teacher) Yes. (Govan) Were you being overpaid? (Teacher) No, it’s a benchmark of a government pay. (Govan) So, what could be the reason for wanting to drop your salary if it’s not inflated? (Teacher) The fact that maybe the company does not have money. (Govan) The retrenchees were told the business faces a crisis, and they still haven’t been paid out. (Govan) How can you face a crisis if you knew how much it would cost and Transnet believed you have the money to run this school? (Dr Maharaswa) Yes, and it is still the case, but our projections are that if we continued with that dispensation, running the school is going to require much more than twenty million. (Chippa subtitles) Everything here is on my shoulders. Okay, teachers? I don’t get any subsidy, no allowance from government; nothing! (Govan) Tough financial decisions make sense in a corporate environment, but in a school, cost-cutting impacts the children. And given what we’re about to tell you, it’s clear who’s paying the price. (Parent) The food is too little. You can't even see the chicken, which part of the chicken they are eating. (Govan) Chipcor got the school on condition all boys already enrolled would continue to be fully sponsored. That’s why their parents are afraid to complain openly. (Parent) My son sent me a picture of two Weetbix without milk. Most of the time they have two-minute noodles with a little bit of veggies in there. (Dr Maharaswa) They stay for free. They eat for free, four meals per day. (Govan) Are they eating two-minute noodles? (Dr Maharaswa) No, actually the noodles is what we see elsewhere. (Govan) On a guided tour of the pantry, we couldn’t help noticing an empty box of instant noodles. Parents of newly enrolled boys are now paying R97 000 a year. But who’s teaching them? (Dr Maharaswa) Qualified educators with relevant specialisations. (Govan) Are these teachers who are fresh out of university or do they have experience teaching? (Dr Maharaswa) The majority of them are fresh out of university. (Govan) How much are you paying the new teachers? (Dr Maharaswa) R16 000 per month. (Govan) Is that an entry-level salary for a teacher? (Dr Maharaswa) It is, it is. (Gertina van der Merwe) You can't pay a teacher peanuts and expect high performance. (Govan) After a heated argument with Dr Maharaswa, Mrs van der Merwe was given a disciplinary hearing and summarily dismissed. (Gertina van der Merwe) My honest opinion is that the kids are going to fail. (Parent) You want now cheap labour, cheap labour that will come with a risk of our children’s education. (Govan) The matrics only received their Term One reports this week, and the Gauteng Department of Education is investigating if the curriculum has been covered. But there’s a more serious matter. (Govan) All independent schools in South Africa have to be registered and accredited with Umalusi, the Council for Quality Assurance. When a school has a change ownership, principal, or its name, Umalusi has to be notified within 14 days. That never happened in this case, which means the Africa School of Excellence is not accredited. (Govan) The school is still relying on the original registration and there’s a photocopy of the certificate hanging in the entrance hall. (Govan) Why didn't you notify Umalusi about the change of ownership and the change of name of the school? (Dr Maharaswa) But there has not been a change of ownership of this entity. (Govan) There has been a change of ownership. (Dr Maharaswa) No. (Govan) Chipcor Developers owns the school. (Dr Maharaswa) No, they operate the school. (Govan) Who owns the school? (Dr Maharaswa) Pardon? (Govan) Who owns the school? (Dr Maharaswa) It's the same entity that it used to own, but we’re operating the school. (Govan) And the school's name has not changed? (Dr Maharaswa) Pardon? The school's name has not...the school's registered name has not changed. We are changing the trading name. (Govan) If you've been charging school fees for this school that's not accredited with Umalusi, that would be fraud. (Dr Maharaswa) That would be, but luckily our school is accredited with Umalusi. (Govan) But accreditation is not transferable between different owners, and Umalusi told Carte Blanche that Africa School of Excellence is not currently accredited. (Govan) But Dr Maharaswa herself is associated with fraud and corruption, after an R11.2 million contract was improperly awarded to her company Northern Lights 371. Her business partner’s uncle was CEO of the SETA at the time and was fired after an investigation. (Govan) Have you ever been accused of fraud personally? (Dr Maharaswa) I don’t think that’s relevant to the interview. The interview is about the school. (Govan) We believe that you’ve been banned from doing tenders with the State for ten years. Is that right? (Dr Maharaswa) That is a matter that is being challenged. It’s under review. (Govan) When Transnet put out requests for proposals, one of its conditions was successful bidder’s tax matters be in order. It’s been widely reported that Chippa Mpengesi owes SARS R53 million in unpaid taxes. We wanted to ask Transnet how they did their due diligence, but they declined an interview. (Govan) Chippa has called those reports misleading, but Transnet confirmed that during the tender process they flagged a matter related to his tax compliance. (Govan) Transnet say they had a robust, open and competitive procurement process, but they deny that Chippa Training Academy submitted a bid for the school. This contradicts their own tender records submitted to Treasury. (Govan) Transnet say they are transferring the relevant assets to Chipcor, but do they mean the vehicles and school equipment, or the buildings and the 12-hectare property? (Govan) Carte Blanche has now requested the full record of decision on this tender, to understand why a hundred schoolboys were entrusted to the care of this flamboyant, but compromised personality. (Govan) Chippa never responded to our interview request.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We take a deep dive into the newly named Africa School of Excellence, and find out why former staff and parents are blowing the whistle on Chippa Mpengesi.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Transnet Football School of Excellence in Kempton Park has been handed over to controversial businessman and Chippa FC owner, Chippa Mpengesi. In just two months, the once proud legacy of this birthplace of champions has been decimated. Staff and coaches have been fired, salaries have not paid, and the boys were left sleeping on the floor, eating 2-minute noodles.
metadata.Summary: Transnet School of Excellence was founded in 1994 as a joint venture between Transnet and SAFA, run by a Board of Trustees. The Trustees included Transnet, SAFA, SAFCOC, Department of Basic Education, a representative of the Community and a representative of the Private Sector. In 2020 the Trust was dissolved and the school was taken over by the Transnet Foundation as part of its CSI responsibilities. Transnet donated R20 m annually to run the school. Last year they decided they could not continue and put out a call for new sponsors. Some sponsors stepped forward and requested Financial Records for the school. NO FINANCIALS AVAILABLE. In August 2025 they published a tender as Request for Proposals, asking for a donor to take over the SOE. They had five bids, including Pitso Mosimane who runs a very successful academy partnering with Curro schools; Thulani Majola a controversial businessman who was previously in liquidation, and Chippa Training Academy (Pty) Ltd, a company belonging to Chippa Mpengesi. One of the criteria was a proven track record educating high school pupils. But, the Chippa Training Academy is a company that trains security guards. What due diligence did Transnet do? The only evidence of a school is social media calls for enrolment at the Chippa Academy in East London in July 2025. The school never opened. Instead, those pupils from the Eastern Cape have been bused to the Germiston campus.
metadata.Further information: The school was handed over on 8 December 2025 amidst much fanfare. It only opened on 26 January as they were renovating the hostels. The teachers were paid late with no payslips, and no deductions. They went to the CCMA and were subsequently fired. The matric students only started classed in the 2nd week of February. Last week every teacher and coach was asked to take a 95% salary reduction or face retrenchment. Everyone, including the Principal, was “retrenched”. There is a new school Manager called Dr Maharaswa, a former Deputy DG at the Department of Basic Education. She has been banned from tendering for government contracts until 2030 because of fraud and corruption at the MICTSETA. She is now in charge of the school, accompanied by an armed bodyguard. Many parents have removed their children, and those that remain are now expected to buy uniforms manufactured by Chippa’s company RADA at a cost of R5000. They are also expected to pay school fees of R9200 per month. Previously this was a school for underprivileged, hugely talented kids, and everything was free. Apart from the "elite football academy", the school claims to offer "Academic Excellence. Core subjects and enrichment programs that challenge learners and prepare them for top-tier universities." But just last week Chippa was heard telling the boys they should become security guards.
